nameStory: Wood nettle gets its name from its preference for woodland habitats, distinguishing it from its more famous cousin, stinging nettle, which prefers open sunny areas. Like other nettles, it earned the 'nettle' part of its name from the Old English 'netel,' meaning 'to sting' - a warning about those tiny hairs that pack a punch! The scientific name Laportea honors French naturalist François Louis de Laporte.
description: Wood nettle is a leafy herbaceous plant that grows 2-4 feet tall in the understory of moist woodlands. It has broad, heart-shaped leaves with prominent veins and serrated edges that give it a somewhat tropical appearance. The plant produces small, inconspicuous greenish flowers in branched clusters, and like other nettles, it's covered in stinging hairs that can cause a burning sensation when touched. It can be either annual or perennial depending on growing conditions.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, heart-shaped leaves with pointed tips and coarsely toothed edges, arranged alternately on the stem. The leaves feel soft but are covered in tiny stinging hairs that create a burning sensation when touched.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers arranged in loose, branched clusters that emerge from the leaf joints. The flowers lack petals and are easy to overlook - they look more like small green beads than typical flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows upright in patches, typically 2-4 feet tall with a bushy appearance. The stems are somewhat succulent and light green, often with a slightly translucent quality.

idTips.label: Stinging Hairs
idTips.description: The entire plant is covered in tiny, needle-like hairs that inject irritating chemicals when broken. These hairs are most noticeable on leaf undersides and stems - they feel like getting tiny glass splinters.

habitat: Wood nettle thrives in rich, moist woodland soils, particularly in areas with good drainage like stream banks, ravines, and forest edges. You'll often find it growing alongside wild ginger, mayapple, and other shade-loving woodland wildflowers in deciduous and mixed forests. It prefers areas that stay consistently moist but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring, starting small and heart-shaped. Young plants are already equipped with stinging hairs, so handle with care even in spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full-sized leaves and tiny greenish flowers appearing in loose clusters. This is when the plant is most robust and the stinging sensation is strongest.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow before dying back. Seeds develop in small clusters, and the plant begins to die back to the ground after the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Completely dies back to the ground, leaving no above-ground parts visible. Perennial roots remain dormant underground in suitable locations.

funFact: The sting of wood nettle can actually be neutralized by rubbing the affected area with the juice from jewelweed (spotted touch-me-not), which often grows nearby - nature's own first aid kit growing side by side!
confusionNotes: Wood nettle is most commonly confused with stinging nettle, but wood nettle has alternate leaves (one per node) while stinging nettle has opposite leaves (two per node). Remember: 'Wood nettle wanders' (alternate arrangement) while 'stinging nettle stays paired' (opposite arrangement).
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name similarity and stinging ability, wood nettle belongs to a different genus than the more common stinging nettle (Urtica), though both are in the nettle family. Many people assume all stinging plants in the woods are poison ivy, but wood nettle's heart-shaped single leaves and upright growth habit are completely different from poison ivy's three-leaflet pattern.
compareHints: Wood nettle is the only member of its genus (Laportea) found in New England, making it unique among our local nettles. Compared to stinging nettle (Urtica species), wood nettle has much broader, heart-shaped leaves arranged alternately rather than opposite, and it prefers shaded woodland habitats instead of sunny disturbed areas. The stinging sensation is similar between the two, but wood nettle's tropical-looking foliage makes it easy to distinguish once you know what to look for.
